'''brawlingly''' (brâ′ling-li), ''adv.'' In a brawling or quarrelsome manner.

'''brawlins''' (brâ′linz), ''adv.'' Same as ''brawly.'' [Scotch.]

'''brawly''' (brâ′li), ''adv.'' and ''a.'' [Also ''brawlie;'' = E. ''bravely.''] Bravely; finely; heartily; very well; in good health or condition. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|I am ''brawly'' now again—it was nae great thing that ailed me.
{{right|''Scott'', Abbot, II. 82.}}}}

'''brawn''' (brân), ''n.'' [< ME. ''braun, brawn,'' muscle, boar’s flesh, < OF. ''braon,'' a piece of flesh, = Pr. ''bradon, brazon, braon'' = OSp. ''brahon,'' < OHG. ''brāto'' (acc. ''brāton''), a piece of flesh for roasting, MHG. ''brāte,'' G. ''braten,'' roast meat (= AS. ''brǣde,'' roast meat), < OHG. ''brātan,'' MHG. ''brāten,'' G. ''braten'' = AS. ''brǣdan'' = OFries. ''brēda'' = D. ''braden,'' roast, broil (cf. Dan. ''brad,'' a joint of meat); cf. Gr. πρήθειν, burn, blow into a flame.] '''1.''' Boar’s flesh; the flesh of the boar or of swine, collared so as to squeeze out much of the fat, boiled, and pickled.
{{smaller block|I see nothing here like Christmas, excepting ''brawn'' and mincepies in places where I dine.
{{right|''Swift'', Journal to Stella, Letter 38.}}}}
'''2.''' A boar. ''Beau. and Fl.'' [Now only prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Bulle-nekkyde was that bierne, and brade in the scholders, Brok-brestede as a ''brawne'' with brustils fulle large.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1095.}}}}
readings.c2s2:
{{smaller block|{{right|''Locke'', Education, § 113.}}}}

'''brawny''' (brâ′ni), ''a.'' [< ME. ''brawny'', fleshy (of fruit); < ''brawn'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Fleshy; muscular; having large strong muscles; bulky; strong.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oxe dounge about her rootes yf that me trete
The pomes sadde and ''brawny'' wol it gete.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', iii. 106.}}
<poem>The muscles of his ''brawny'' arms
Are strong as iron bands.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Village Blacksmith.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, firm; hardened; having great power of resistance.
{{smaller block|A ''brawny'' conscience which hath no feeling in it.
{{right|''J. Mede'', Apost. of the Latter Times, ii.}}}}

'''braws''' (brâz), ''n. pl.'' See ''braw'', ''n.''

'''braxy''' (brak′si), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [E. dial., Sc. also ''braxes'', ''braxit'', also ''bracks'', ''braik''. Cf. ''brack''<sup>1</sup> and ''brash''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A disease of sheep characterized by inflammation of the bowels and retention of the urine: also called ''the sickness'' in some parts of Scotland. The name is also given to a variety of other diseases of sheep.—'''2.''' A sheep having the braxy; hence, the mutton of such a sheep.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Affected or tainted with braxy: as, ''braxy'' sheep; ''braxy'' mutton.

Also spelled ''braksy.''

'''bray'''<sup>1</sup> (brā), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''brayen'', < OF. ''brayer'', ''breier'', ''brehier'', F. ''broyer'' = Pr. Sp. ''bregar'', pound, bray, prob. < MHG. ''brechen'' = E. ''break'', q. v.] To pound or beat thoroughly, as with a pestle or other instrument; triturate, crush, mix, etc., by beating or any analogous action: as, to ''bray'' drugs; to ''bray'' printers’ ink. See ''brayer''<sup>1</sup>.
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''bray<sup>5</sup>''' (brā), ''n.'' [Also written ''brey''; < F. ''braye'', “a close linnen breek or under-slop, . . . also a clout,” pl. ''brayes'', “short and close breeches, drawers, or under-hose of linnen, &c.,” . . . also “barnacles for a horse’s nose” (Cotgrave), mod. F. ''braies'', breeches, < L. ''bracæ'', breeches: see ''bracæ'', ''brail'', and ''breech''.] '''1†.''' A clout for a young child. ''Kersey'', 1708.—'''2.''' In ''her.'': (''a'') Barnacles or twitchers for subduing a horse: used as a bearing. (''b'') [Perhaps a corruption of ''brake''<sup>3</sup>, ''break''.] A bearing similar to the preceding in form, representing a tool used for breaking hemp: sometimes called a ''hemp-bray'', ''hemp-brake'', or ''hackle''. {{smaller|One or other of these bearings is frequently used in allusive heraldry for families of the name ''Bray'' and the like.}}

'''brayd''', '''brayde†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''braid''.

'''brayer<sup>1</sup>''' (brā′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''bray''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] In ''printing'', a small composition-roller used for triturating and spreading the ink on a table or slab and daubing it on a platen or disk.

'''brayer<sup>2</sup>''' (brā′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''bray''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who or that which brays like an ass.

'''Brayera''' (bra-yē′rä), ''n.'' [NL.] See ''Hagenia''.

'''brayette''' (bra-yet′), ''n.'' [F.] Same as ''braguette''.

'''braying''' (brā′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brayinge''; verbal n. of ''bray''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The harsh crying of an ass.—'''2.''' Vocal or instrumental clamor; harsh utterance.
{{smaller block|There he stands with unimpeachable passivity amid the shouldering and ''braying''; a spectacle to men.
{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. v. 2.}}}}

'''braylet†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''brail.''

'''braynet†''', ''n.'' See ''brain.''

'''braze<sup>1</sup>''' (brāz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''brazed'', ppr. ''brazing.'' [< ME. ''brasen'', < AS. ''brasian'', cover with brass, < ''bræs'', brass: see ''brass''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''glaze'', < ''glass''; ''graze'', < ''grass.''] To cover or ornament with brass, or as if with brass: as, “a tripod richly ''brazed'',” ''Chapman'', Odyssey, xv.
{{smaller block|<poem>Show of clouds
That ''braze'' the horizon’s western rim.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}}}

'''braze<sup>2</sup>''' (brāz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''brazed'', ppr. ''brazing.'' [< F. ''braser'', OF. ''braser'', solder, < Icel. ''brasa'', harden by fire: see ''brass''<sup>1</sup> and ''braize''<sup>1</sup>. Partly confused with ''braze''<sup>1</sup>, from the same ult. source.] '''1.''' To solder, especially with hard solder, such as an alloy of brass and zinc.
{{smaller block|In the reign of Henry IV. it was enacted that all arrowheads should be well ''brased'' and hardened at the points with steel. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', II. 372.}}}}
'''2†.''' To harden; make callous.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let me wring your heart: for so I shall, . . .
If damned custom hath not ''braz’d'' it so,
That it is proof and bulwark against sense.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4.}}}}

'''braze<sup>3</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''braize''<sup>2</sup>, 2.

'''brazed''' (brāzd), ''a.'' In ''her.'', same as ''braced'', 1.

'''brazen''' (brā′zn), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''brasen'', < ME. ''brasen'', < AS. ''bræsen'', of brass, < ''bræs'', brass, + ''-en''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Made of brass: as, a ''brazen'' helmet.—'''2.''' Pertaining to brass; proceeding from brass.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|brawl|666|'''brazen'''}}</noinclude>''bray''<sup>2</sup>. The ult. source of all these forms is perhaps the same. See ''brag''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To speak loudly and complainingly or angrily; be clamorous or noisy; quarrel noisily and indecently.
{{smaller block|I do the wrong, and first begin to ''brawl''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To roar, as water flowing over a pebbly or rocky bed; make a loud babbling noise.
{{smaller block|The brook that ''brawls'' along this wood.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Crossing the brook at the ford, where it ''brawled'' over pebble and shallow.
{{right|''Longfellow'', Miles Standish, iii.}}}}
{{smaller|=Syn. '''1.''' To wrangle, squabble, dispute (noisily).}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To wrangle about; be noisy or contentious regarding.
{{smaller block|I care not what the sects may ''brawl''.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Palace of Art.}}}}
'''2.''' To drive away or beat down by noise. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Your deep wit . . .
Reason’d, not ''brawl’d'' her [Truth] hence.</poem>
{{right|''Sir K. Digby'', Preface to Nature of Man’s Soul.}}}}

'''brawl'''<sup>1</sup> (brâl), ''n.''   [< ''brawl''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   A noisy quarrel; loud, angry contention; an uproar; row; squabble: as, “stout polemick ''brawl'',” ''S. Butler'', Hudibras.
{{smaller block|He is a devil in private ''brawl''.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|A creature wholly given to ''brawls'' and wine.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}
{{smaller block|The whole world knows that this is no accidental ''brawl'', but a systematic war to the knife, and in defiance of all laws and liberties.
{{right|''Emerson'', Affairs in Kansas.}}}}
{{smaller|=Syn. ''Broil'', ''Affray'', etc. See ''quarrel'', ''n.''}}

'''brawl'''<sup>2</sup> (brâl), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''brall''; a corruption of earlier ''bransle'', also written ''bransel'', ''brantle'', ''brangle'', etc., < F. ''bransle'', now ''branle'', a dance, same as ''bransle'', ''branle'', verbal n. of ''bransler'', ''branler'', shake, move, etc.: see ''brandle'', ''brantle'', ''branle''.]   A kind of dance; a branle.
{{smaller block|<poem>Good fellowes must go learne to daunce,
The brydeal is full near-a;
There is a ''brall'' come out of Fraunce,
The fyrst ye harde this yeare-a.</poem>
{{right|''Good Fellowes'' (1569). (''Halliwell'', Note to Marston’s Plays.)}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thence did Venus learn to lead
The Idalian ''brawls''. ''B. Jonson'', Vision of Delight.</poem>
<poem>My grave lord-keeper led the ''brawls'';
The seal and maces danced before him.</poem>
{{right|''Gray'', Long Story.}}}}

'''brawler''' (brâ′lėr), ''n.''   [ME. ''brawlere''.]   One who brawls; a noisy fellow; a wrangler.
{{smaller block|The great statesman degenerated into an angry ''brawler''.
{{right|''Buckle'', Civilization, I. xii.}}}}

'''brawlie''', ''adv.'' See ''brawly''.

'''brawling''' (brâ′ling), ''n.''   [ME. ''braulyng''; verbal n. of ''brawl''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   The act of quarreling; specifically, in ''Eng. law'', the offense of quarreling or creating a disturbance in a church or churchyard.

'''brawling''' (brâ′ling), ''p. a.''   [Ppr. of ''brawl''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' Contentious; quarrelsome; noisy.
{{smaller block|I know she is an irksome, ''brawling'' scold.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The spirit-grieving sounds of ''brawling'' commerce.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 160.}}}}
{{smaller block|From ''brawling'' parties concords come.
{{right|''Lowell'', To the Muse.}}}}
'''2.''' Making the noise of rushing water: as, “''brawling'' springs,” ''Collins.''
{{smaller block|The ''brawling'' streams shall soon be dumb.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Old-Year Song.}}}}

'''brawlingly''' (brâ′ling-li), ''adv.'' In a brawling or quarrelsome manner.

'''brawlins''' (brâ′linz), ''adv.'' Same as ''brawly.''   [Scotch.]

'''brawly''' (brâ′li), ''adv.'' and ''a.''   [Also ''brawlie;'' = E. ''bravely.'']   Bravely; finely; heartily; very well; in good health or condition. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|I am ''brawly'' now again—it was nae great thing that ailed me.
{{right|''Scott'', Abbot, II. 82.}}}}

'''brawn''' (brân), ''n.''   [< ME. ''braun, brawn,'' muscle, boar’s flesh, < OF. ''braon,'' a piece of flesh, = Pr. ''bradon, brazon, braon'' = OSp. ''brahon,'' < OHG. ''brāto'' (acc. ''brāton''), a piece of flesh for roasting, MHG. ''brāte,'' G. ''braten,'' roast meat (= AS. ''brǣde,'' roast meat), < OHG. ''brātan,'' MHG. ''brāten,'' G. ''braten'' = AS. ''brǣdan'' = OFries. ''brēda'' = D. ''braden,'' roast, broil (cf. Dan. ''brad,'' a joint of meat); cf. Gr. πρήθειν, burn, blow into a flame.]   '''1.''' Boar’s flesh; the flesh of the boar or of swine, collared so as to squeeze out much of the fat, boiled, and pickled.
{{smaller block|I see nothing here like Christmas, excepting ''brawn'' and mincepies in places where I dine.
{{right|''Swift'', Journal to Stella, Letter 38.}}}}
'''2.''' A boar.   ''Beau. and Fl.'' [Now only prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Bulle-nekkyde was that bierne, and brade in the scholders, Brok-brestede as a ''brawne'' with brustils fulle large.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1095.}}}}

'''3.''' The flesh of a muscular part of the body: as, the ''brawn'' of the arm, thigh, etc.
{{smaller block|It was ordained that murtherers should be brent on the ''brawn'' of the left hand.
{{right|''Hall'', Hen. VII., an. 15.}}}}

'''4.''' Well-developed muscles; muscular strength.
{{smaller block|''Brawn'' without brain is thine.
{{right|''Dryden'', Fables.}}}}
{{smaller block|Here, then, is a great stalwart man, in perfect health, all ''brawn'' and rude muscle, set up before us as the ideal of strength.
{{right|''S. Lanier'', The English Novel, p. 54.}}}}

'''5.''' Figuratively, the arm: from its muscles or strength. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll hide my silver beard in a gold beaver,
And in my vantbrace put this wither’d ''brawn.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I had purpose
Once more to hew thy target from thy ''brawn'',
Or lose my arm for’t.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 5.}}}}

'''6.''' Head-cheese.—{{smaller|'''Mock brawn,''' the flesh of a pig’s head and feet cut in pieces, and boiled, pickled, and pressed into a form.}}

'''brawned†''' (brând), ''a.''   [< ''brawn'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Brawny; strong: as, “''brawned'' bowrs,” ''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 41.

'''brawner''' (brâ′nėr), ''n.''   [< ''brawn'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   A boar killed for the table.

'''brawn-fallen†''' (brân′fâ″ln), ''a.'' Having the brawny or muscular parts of the body shrunk or fallen away; wasted; thin; weak.
{{smaller block|Were not Milo his armes ''brawnefallen'' for want of wrastlyng?
{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 127.}}}}

'''brawniness''' (brâ′ni-nes), ''n.''   [< ''brawny'' + ''-ness.'']   The quality of being brawny; strength; hardiness.
{{smaller block|This ''brawniness'' and insensibility of mind is the best armour against the common evils and accidents of life. {{right|''Locke'', Education, § 113.}}}}

'''brawny''' (brâ′ni), ''a.''   [< ME. ''brawny'', fleshy (of fruit); < ''brawn'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Fleshy; muscular; having large strong muscles; bulky; strong.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oxe dounge about her rootes yf that me trete
The pomes sadde and ''brawny'' wol it gete.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', iii. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The muscles of his ''brawny'' arms
Are strong as iron bands.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Village Blacksmith.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, firm; hardened; having great power of resistance.
{{smaller block|A ''brawny'' conscience which hath no feeling in it.
{{right|''J. Mede'', Apost. of the Latter Times, ii.}}}}

'''braws''' (brâz), ''n. pl.'' See ''braw'', ''n.''

'''braxy''' (brak′si), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [E. dial., Sc. also ''braxes'', ''braxit'', also ''bracks'', ''braik''. Cf. ''brack''<sup>1</sup> and ''brash''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A disease of sheep characterized by inflammation of the bowels and retention of the urine: also called ''the sickness'' in some parts of Scotland. The name is also given to a variety of other diseases of sheep.—'''2.''' A sheep having the braxy; hence, the mutton of such a sheep.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Affected or tainted with braxy: as, ''braxy'' sheep; ''braxy'' mutton.

Also spelled ''braksy.''

'''bray'''<sup>1</sup> (brā), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''brayen'', < OF. ''brayer'', ''breier'', ''brehier'', F. ''broyer'' = Pr. Sp. ''bregar'', pound, bray, prob. < MHG. ''brechen'' = E. ''break'', q. v.]   To pound or beat thoroughly, as with a pestle or other instrument; triturate, crush, mix, etc., by beating or any analogous action: as, to ''bray'' drugs; to ''bray'' printers’ ink. See ''brayer''<sup>1</sup>. {{smaller block|Recipe the cromys of whyte brede, & swete apyls, & ȝokkis of eggis, & ''bray'' tham wele.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 53.}}}}
{{smaller block|Though thou shouldst ''bray'' a fool in a mortar, . . . yet will not his foolishness depart from him. Prov. xxvii. 22.}}

'''bray'''<sup>2</sup> (brā), ''v.''   [< ME. ''brayen'', < OF. ''braire'', < ML. ''bragire'', bray, ''bragare'', cry, squall, prob. of Celtic origin: see ''brag'' and ''brawl''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To utter a loud and harsh cry: with reference now especially to the ass, but formerly also to the bull, deer, and other animals, as well as to man.
{{smaller block|Whan the squyers hadde cried and ''braied'' for theire lord longe while, thei toke hym vp and bar hym to theire hostell.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 467.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whan the Sarazin felte hym-self so diffouled, he fledde cryinge and ''brayinge'' as a bole [bull].
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 552.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Laugh, and they
Return it louder than an ass can ''bray''.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' To make a loud, harsh, disagreeable sound.
{{smaller block|Heard ye the din of battle ''bray?'' {{right|''Gray'', The Bard.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And varying notes the war-pipes ''brayed''
To ever varying clan. ''Scott'', Marmion, v. 5.</poem>}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To utter with a loud, harsh sound, like the ass.
{{smaller block|<poem>The kettle-drum and trumpet thus ''bray'' out
The triumph of his pledge. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 4.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Arms on armour clashing ''bray’d''
Horrible discord. ''Milton'', P. L., vi. 209.</poem>}}

'''bray<sup>2</sup>''' (brā), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bray'', a loud cry, also ''brayt'', < OF. ''brait'' = Pr. ''brai''; from the verb.]   A harsh cry, especially that of an ass; hence, any similar harsh or grating sound.
{{smaller block|Several times a day we are stunned and overwhelmed with the cracked ''brays'' of three discordant trumpets.
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Lands of the Saracen, p. 25.}}}}

'''bray<sup>3</sup>†''' (brā), ''n.''   [< OF. ''braie'', a kind of bastion, a dike or bank, < ML. ''braca'', a dike or bank, same as OF. ''braie'', < ML. ''braga'', part of a river confined between dikes to facilitate the catching of fish.]   A bank or mound of earth used in fortification; a breastwork; a bulwark; specifically, a wall or other work in advance of and covering the gate of a fortress.
{{smaller block|That they could scant put their heads over the ''bray'' or bulwark. {{right|''Hall'', Hen. VIII., an. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|Order was given that bulwarks, ''brays'', and walls should be raised in his castles and strongholds.
{{right|''Lord Herbert'', Hen. VIII., p. 28.}}}}

'''bray<sup>4</sup>''' (brā), ''n.''   [= Sc. ''brae'', ''bra'', < ME. ''braye'', also ''bra'', ''bro'', etc., < Gael. ''braigh'', the upper part of any thing or place (''braigh duthcha'', the higher parts of a district; ''braigh Lochabar'', the braes of Lochaber, etc.), also ''braidh'' = Ir. ''braid'', upper part, height; cf. W. ''brig'', top, summit, ''bre'', hill, peak, = AS. ''beorh'', E. ''barrow'', a hill, mound: see ''barrow''<sup>1</sup>.]   A piece of sloping ground; an acclivity or declivity.
{{smaller block|Against a rocke or an hye ''braye''.
{{right|''Ascham'', Toxophilus, Works, p. 170.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Push’d up the ''bray'', indignantly they feel
The clanking lash and the retorted steel.</poem>
{{right|''Brookes'', The Fox-Chase.}}}}

'''bray<sup>5</sup>''' (brā), ''n.''   [Also written ''brey''; < F. ''braye'', “a close linnen breek or under-slop, . . . also a clout,” pl. ''brayes'', “short and close breeches, drawers, or under-hose of linnen, &c.,” . . . also “barnacles for a horse’s nose” (Cotgrave), mod. F. ''braies'', breeches, < L. ''bracæ'', breeches: see ''bracæ'', ''brail'', and ''breech''.]   '''1†.''' A clout for a young child.   ''Kersey'', 1708.—'''2.''' In ''her.'': (''a'') Barnacles or twitchers for subduing a horse: used as a bearing. (''b'') [Perhaps a corruption of ''brake''<sup>3</sup>, ''break''.] A bearing similar to the preceding in form, representing a tool used for breaking hemp: sometimes called a ''hemp-bray'', ''hemp-brake'', or ''hackle''. {{smaller|One or other of these bearings is frequently used in allusive heraldry for families of the name ''Bray'' and the like.}}

'''brayd''', '''brayde†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''braid''.

'''brayer<sup>1</sup>''' (brā′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bray''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   In ''printing'', a small composition-roller used for triturating and spreading the ink on a table or slab and daubing it on a platen or disk.

'''brayer<sup>2</sup>''' (brā′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bray''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who or that which brays like an ass.

'''Brayera''' (bra-yē′rä), ''n.''   [NL.]   See ''Hagenia''.

'''brayette''' (bra-yet′), ''n.''   [F.]   Same as ''braguette''.

'''braying''' (brā′ing), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brayinge''; verbal n. of ''bray''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' The harsh crying of an ass.—'''2.''' Vocal or instrumental clamor; harsh utterance.
{{smaller block|There he stands with unimpeachable passivity amid the shouldering and ''braying''; a spectacle to men.
{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. v. 2.}}}}

'''braylet†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''brail.''

'''braynet†''', ''n.'' See ''brain.''

'''braze<sup>1</sup>''' (brāz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''brazed'', ppr. ''brazing.''   [< ME. ''brasen'', < AS. ''brasian'', cover with brass, < ''bræs'', brass: see ''brass''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''glaze'', < ''glass''; ''graze'', < ''grass.'']   To cover or ornament with brass, or as if with brass: as, “a tripod richly ''brazed'',” ''Chapman'', Odyssey, xv.
{{smaller block|<poem>Show of clouds
That ''braze'' the horizon’s western rim.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}}}

'''braze<sup>2</sup>''' (brāz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''brazed'', ppr. ''brazing.''   [< F. ''braser'', OF. ''braser'', solder, < Icel. ''brasa'', harden by fire: see ''brass''<sup>1</sup> and ''braize''<sup>1</sup>. Partly confused with ''braze''<sup>1</sup>, from the same ult. source.]   '''1.''' To solder, especially with hard solder, such as an alloy of brass and zinc.
{{smaller block|In the reign of Henry IV. it was enacted that all arrowheads should be well ''brased'' and hardened at the points with steel. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', II. 372.}}}}
'''2†.''' To harden; make callous.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let me wring your heart: for so I shall, . . .
If damned custom hath not ''braz’d'' it so,
That it is proof and bulwark against sense.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4.}}}}

'''braze<sup>3</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''braize''<sup>2</sup>, 2.

'''brazed''' (brāzd), ''a.'' In ''her.'', same as ''braced'', 1.

'''brazen''' (brā′zn), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''brasen'', < ME. ''brasen'', < AS. ''bræsen'', of brass, < ''bræs'', brass, + ''-en''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Made of brass: as, a ''brazen'' helmet.—'''2.''' Pertaining to brass; proceeding from brass.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
